summary: Paul G. Hackett is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He succeeded Richard B. Martin at the University of Virginia, where he served as a bibliographer and curator, and later held research and lecturer positions at Columbia University.

Paul Groner is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Japanology who earned his PhD from Yale University and studied at the University of Tokyo in 1973. He held long-term professorial and faculty posts at the University of Virginia.

Paul Hacker (1913–1979) was a scholar of Indology, philosophy, and religious studies. Educated at Bonn, Heidelberg, Frankfurt, and Berlin, he held posts at Mithila Research Institute, University of Bonn, and the University of Münster.

Paul Harrison (born 1950) specializes in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He completed his MA at the University of Auckland and PhD at the Australian National University under Jan Willem de Jong, later holding faculty appointments at Canterbury and Stanford.

Paul J. Griffiths (born 1955) works in Buddhist studies, religious studies, and philosophy. Educated at Oxford and Wisconsin-Madison under Minoru Kiyota, he held professorships at the University of Chicago, Notre Dame, University of Illinois Chicago, and Duke University.
Paul K. Nietupski works in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He earned his PhD at Columbia University and held an attested post at John Carroll University in 2008.
Paul Kingsbury is a scholar in linguistics and Indology. He completed his PhD at the University of Pennsylvania under the supervision of George Cardona.

Paul Kiparsky (born 1941) is a linguist and Indologist. He earned his degree at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he studied under Morris Halle, and joined the faculty at Stanford University around 1984.

Paul L. Swanson (born 1951) works in Buddhist studies, religious studies, and Japanology. He studied at Otani University and earned his PhD from the University of Wisconsin-Madison under Minoru Kiyota, later serving as a professor at Nanzan University.

Paul Mendes-Flohr (1941–2024) was a scholar of religious studies and philosophy who studied at Brooklyn College and Brandeis University. He served as a director at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and held a professorship at the University of Chicago.

Paul Mus (1902–1969) studied Buddhist studies, religious studies, and history/archaeology at EPHE, INALCO, and the University of Paris. His career included posts at EFEO, EPHE, École nationale de la France d'outre-mer, Yale, and the Collège de France.
Paul Passy (1859–1940) was a linguist who studied under Ferdinand de Saussure. He held an academic post at the École Pratique des Hautes Études from approximately 1894 to 1913.

Paul Pelliot (1878–1945) was a scholar of Sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Tibetology, educated at Paris, Sorbonne, and INALCO. He held professorships at the École française d'Extrême-Orient and the Collège de France.

Paul R. Brass (1936–2022) specialized in Indology. He studied at Harvard College, Harvard University, and the University of Chicago, and spent his career as a professor at the University of Washington.
Paul Regnaud (1838–1910) was an Indologist and linguist. He studied as an élève at the École Pratique des Hautes Études and served on the faculty at the University of Lyon from around 1879 to 1908.

Paul Ricœur (1913–2005) was a philosopher and religious studies scholar educated at Rennes and the University of Paris. He held major posts at Strasbourg, Paris Nanterre, Université catholique de Louvain, and the University of Chicago.
Paul Rouzer is a scholar in the fields of Sinology and Buddhist studies. He held attested academic appointments at Harvard University and the University of Minnesota in 2007.

Paul Tedesco (1898–1980) was a scholar of Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. Educated at the University of Vienna, he worked in research at Princeton and served as a professor at Yale University.

Paul Thieme (1905–2001) studied Indology and linguistics at Göttingen and Berlin. He held professorships at the universities of Breslau, Halle-Wittenberg, Frankfurt, and Tübingen, as well as the Edward E. Salisbury chair at Yale University.

Paul Tillich (1886–1965) studied at Berlin, Tübingen, Halle-Wittenberg, and Breslau. He held professorships at TU Dresden, Frankfurt, Union Theological Seminary, Harvard University, and the University of Chicago in theology, philosophy, and sociology.
